notes.front: What is a network topology?
notes.back: The way a network’s nodes are joined to one another by links: which devices connect to which.
notes.explanation: The IETF’s model for describing topologies starts from a list of nodes and adds the links between them, and the points where each link ends.
notes.example: Like a seating plan that shows who sits next to whom, but for which devices link to which.
notes.source: RFC 8345, A YANG Data Model for Network Topologies, §1 Introduction, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a peer-to-peer (P2P) network?
notes.back: A network in which every participant can communicate with the others without going through a central point.
notes.explanation: With no central point there are multiple pathways, so the loss of any one participant does not prevent communication.
notes.example: Like colleagues passing files from desk to desk, but with no central file server in between.
notes.source: NISTIR 8202, Blockchain Technology Overview, Appendix B Glossary, “Distributed network”, PDF p. 62
notes.evidence: A network configuration where every network participant can communicate with one another without going through a centralized point. Since there are multiple pathways for communication, the loss of any participant will not prevent communication. This is also known as a peer-to-peer network.

notes.front: What is a client-server system?
notes.back: One in which client workstations connect to servers, with processing and data possible at both the server and the client.
notes.explanation: NIST’s contingency guide adds that clients are normally desktop computers, although portable devices may also connect to servers as clients.
notes.example: Like staff laptops opening mail that sits on the office mail server.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, §5.2 Client/Server Systems, PDF p. 62
notes.evidence: Client/server systems can have processing and data at both the server and client workstation levels. Client workstations are normally desktop computers, although portable devices may be connected to servers as clients.

notes.front: What is software-defined networking (SDN)?
notes.back: Networking that leaves packet forwarding on the switches but moves the routing decisions to one central controller.
notes.explanation: A traditional switch does both jobs itself; SDN splits them, keeping forwarding at the switch and routing at the controller.
notes.example: Like air traffic control: each aircraft still flies itself, but a central tower decides the routes.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, Appendix E.1.4 Software-Defined Networking (SDN), PDF p. 225
notes.evidence: Traditional networking switches are responsible for both forwarding packets (data plane) and running the distributed algorithms that determine routing (control plane). SDN is a technology that evolves this concept by keeping the data plane at the switch and moving the control plane to a centralized controller.

notes.front: What is a software-defined wide-area network (SD-WAN)?
notes.back: A wide-area network technology that separates the network’s control plane from its data plane, so policies can be set centrally.
notes.explanation: NIST links its adoption to the advent of virtualisation and to increasing enterprise access to cloud services.
notes.example: Like managing all of a company’s branch-office links from one screen instead of configuring each link by hand.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, §5 Secure SD-WAN, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: SD-WAN technology removes the tight coupling between the control plane and data plane functions of the network and enables the centralized specification of various policies, such as access control, routing, and application traffic prioritization.

notes.front: What is the User Datagram Protocol (UDP)?
notes.back: A commonly used transport-layer protocol that provides unreliable, connectionless communications.
notes.explanation: NIST sets it beside TCP, the other common transport protocol, which instead provides reliable connection-oriented communications.
notes.example: Like sending postcards: each goes on its own, with no call set up first and no receipt.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, §2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: TCP, which provides reliable connection-oriented communications, and the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), which provides unreliable connectionless communications, are commonly used transport layer protocols.

notes.front: What is Secure Shell (SSH)?
notes.back: A secure protocol for communicating with a system to administer it over the network.
notes.explanation: NIST names it beside TLS as a secure protocol for administrators to communicate with the systems they manage.
notes.example: Like a locked phone line to a server’s console, carried over the network.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125A Rev. 1, Security Recommendations for Server-based Hypervisor Platforms, §7 Security Recommendations for HY-BF5, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: Communicating with the hypervisor through a secure protocol such as TLS or Secure Shell (SSH)

notes.front: As data passes down the TCP/IP layers to be sent, what does each layer do to it?
notes.back: Adds more information: the data a layer produces is encapsulated in a larger container by the layer below.
notes.explanation: The lowest layer then sends the accumulated data through the physical network, and at the destination the data is passed back up through the layers.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2 Overview of Firewall Technologies, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: the data is passed from the highest layer through intermediate layers to the lowest layer, with each layer adding more information. The lowest layer sends the accumulated data through the physical network, with the data then passed upwards through the layers to its destination.

notes.front: At which TCP/IP layer does Ethernet work?
notes.back: The hardware layer, also known as the data link layer.
notes.explanation: This layer handles communications on the physical network components, and NIST calls Ethernet its best-known protocol.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2 Overview of Firewall Technologies, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: Hardware Layer (also known as the Data Link Layer). This layer handles communications on the physical network components. The best known data link layer protocol is Ethernet.

notes.front: At which layer are media access control (MAC) addresses used, and what are they assigned to?
notes.back: The data link layer; they are assigned to network interfaces, such as an Ethernet card.
notes.explanation: NIST’s example is an Ethernet address that belongs to an Ethernet card.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2 Overview of Firewall Technologies, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: Addresses at the data link layer, which are assigned to network interfaces, are referred to as media access control (MAC) addresses—an example of this is an Ethernet address that belongs to an Ethernet card.

notes.front: Besides IP itself, what are two protocols that NIST places at the network layer?
notes.back: The Internet Control Message Protocol and the Internet Group Management Protocol.
notes.explanation: The network layer routes packets across networks, and IP is its fundamental protocol for TCP/IP.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, §2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: Network Layer. This layer routes packets across networks. IP is the fundamental network layer protocol for TCP/IP. Other commonly used protocols at the network layer are the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) and the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP).

notes.front: Which layers of the OSI stack can a next-generation firewall examine?
notes.back: Layers 3 and 4, and also layer 7, the application level.
notes.explanation: NIST calls application data awareness the distinguishing feature of this kind of firewall.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, §3.1 Firewalls, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: The distinguishing feature of NGFW is application data awareness. It can look at data not only at layers 3 and 4 of an Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) stack but also at layer 7 – the application level.

notes.front: A small office’s router is set to drop packets using only their source and destination addresses and protocol, with no view of their contents. At which layer does this basic packet filter operate?
notes.back: B: The network layer.
notes.choices:
A) The application layer
B) The network layer
C) The hardware (data link) layer
D) The session layer
notes.choicesExplained: A: packet filters are not concerned with the content of packets, which is where application data lies. C: the data link layer is where MAC addresses live, and firewall policies rarely concern themselves with it. D: the session layer sits above the network layer; addresses and protocol, which this filter reads, are network-layer information.
notes.explanation: NIST says firewalls with packet filters, in their most basic form, operate at the network layer.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2.1.1 Packet Filtering, PDF p. 12
notes.evidence: In their most basic form, firewalls with packet filters operate at the network layer.

notes.front: In a centralised network configuration, what happens if the central authority is lost?
notes.back: No participant can communicate, because every participant must go through that single source.
notes.explanation: In this configuration participants must communicate with a central authority to reach one another.
notes.source: NISTIR 8202, Blockchain Technology Overview, Appendix B Glossary, “Centralized network”, PDF p. 61
notes.evidence: communicate with a central authority to communicate with one another. Since all participants must go through a single centralized source, the loss of that source would prevent all participants from communicating.

notes.front: What is a decentralised network configuration, and what does losing one hub do?
notes.back: Several authorities each act as a central hub for a subsection of participants; losing a hub cuts off only that hub’s participants.
notes.explanation: Only the participants behind that hub depend on it.
notes.source: NISTIR 8202, Blockchain Technology Overview, Appendix B Glossary, “Decentralized network”, PDF p. 62
notes.evidence: are multiple authorities that serve as a centralized hub for a subsection of participants. Since some participants are behind a centralized hub, the loss of that hub will prevent those participants from communicating.

notes.front: In a club’s messaging system, every member’s message passes through one server at the clubhouse. When that server fails, nobody can message anyone. Which network configuration is this?
notes.back: B: Centralised.
notes.choices:
A) Distributed (peer-to-peer)
B) Centralised
C) Decentralised
notes.choicesExplained: A: in a distributed network participants reach each other without a central point, so one failure would not silence everyone. C: in a decentralised network, losing a hub cuts off only the participants behind that hub.
notes.explanation: All participants depend on a single central source, so losing it prevents all of them from communicating.
notes.source: NISTIR 8202, Blockchain Technology Overview, Appendix B Glossary, “Centralized network”, PDF p. 61
notes.evidence: Since all participants must go through a single centralized source, the loss of that source would prevent all participants from communicating.

notes.front: A charity runs three regional hub servers, and each hub relays messages for the offices in its region. One hub fails: its region’s offices go quiet, but the other regions carry on. Which network configuration is this?
notes.back: A: Decentralised.
notes.choices:
A) Decentralised
B) Centralised
C) Distributed (peer-to-peer)
notes.choicesExplained: B: in a centralised network, losing the one central source would silence every office. C: in a distributed network, offices would not depend on any hub, so none would go quiet.
notes.explanation: Several authorities each serve a subsection of participants, so a hub failure cuts off only those behind it.
notes.source: NISTIR 8202, Blockchain Technology Overview, Appendix B Glossary, “Decentralized network”, PDF p. 62
notes.evidence: Since some participants are behind a centralized hub, the loss of that hub will prevent those participants from communicating.

notes.front: Which three protocols does NIST’s least functionality control give as examples of unsecure protocols?
notes.back: Bluetooth, the File Transfer Protocol, and peer-to-peer networking.
notes.explanation: Organisations may judge a protocol’s security themselves or rely on other entities’ assessments; these three are NIST’s examples of unsecure ones.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls, CM-7(1) Least Functionality | Periodic Review, PDF p. 132
notes.evidence: Organizations can either decide the relative security of the function, port, protocol, and/or service or base the security decision on the assessment of other entities. Unsecure protocols include Bluetooth, FTP, and peer-to-peer networking.

notes.front: An assessor is examining a company’s firewall ruleset. Company policy bans file-sharing apps that swap files directly between users’ machines. What should the assessor check?
notes.back: B: That the ruleset complies with the policy on prohibited activities such as peer-to-peer file sharing.
notes.choices:
A) That the ruleset permits all outbound traffic, so users are not blocked
B) That the ruleset complies with the policy on prohibited activities such as peer-to-peer file sharing
C) Nothing: file sharing is an application matter, not a firewall one
D) That the firewall has the latest hardware
notes.choicesExplained: A: permitting everything would ignore the policy the ruleset should enforce. D: hardware age is not what a ruleset review examines. C: NIST gives peer-to-peer file sharing as an example of what a firewall ruleset review covers.
notes.explanation: NIST’s testing guide gives exactly this as an example of an examination: checking a firewall’s ruleset against policies on internet use.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-115, Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment, §2.1 Assessment Methodologies… Examination, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: Another example is reviewing a firewall’s ruleset to ensure its compliance with the organization’s security policies regarding Internet usage, such as the use of instant messaging, peer-to-peer (P2P) file sharing, and other prohibited activities.

notes.front: A blockchain network has nodes in many countries and works peer-to-peer. A power cut takes every node in one region offline. What happens to the network?
notes.back: A: It keeps working, because it is resilient to losing any node or even a whole region.
notes.choices:
A) It keeps working, because it is resilient to losing any node or even a whole region
B) It stops until the region’s central server returns
C) Only nodes in the same region as the central hub stop
D) It stops, because every node must be online for any to communicate
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: a peer-to-peer network has no central server or hub that others depend on. D: with multiple pathways, the loss of some participants does not prevent communication.
notes.explanation: NIST says geographic spread, together with peer-to-peer working, makes such a network resilient to the loss of any node or region.
notes.source: NISTIR 8202, Blockchain Technology Overview, §3.8 Blockchain Network Properties…, PDF p. 25
notes.evidence: Because of this, and the blockchain network working in a peer-to-peer fashion, it is resilient to the loss of any node, or even an entire region of nodes.

notes.front: Peer-to-peer versus centralised network: how do participants reach each other, and what does one failure do?
notes.back: Peer-to-peer: directly, over many pathways, so losing one participant stops nothing. Centralised: through one central authority, whose loss stops everyone.
notes.explanation: The difference is whether any single point sits between every pair of participants.
notes.source: NISTIR 8202, Blockchain Technology Overview, Appendix B Glossary, PDF p. 62
notes.evidence: Since there are multiple pathways for communication, the loss of any participant will not prevent communication. This is also known as a peer-to-peer network.

notes.front: In a client-server system, what are two services the servers support?
notes.back: Any two of: file sharing and storage; central application hosting, such as email; user authentication, among others.
notes.explanation: NIST’s list also includes data processing, printing, access control and remote access connectivity.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, §5.2 Client/Server Systems, PDF p. 62
notes.evidence: Servers support file sharing and storage, data processing, central application hosting (such as email or a central database), printing, access control, user authentication, remote access connectivity, and other

notes.front: At a school, staff sign in at networked desktop PCs to reach shared folders and the timetable app, all held on machines in the server room. Which relationship is this?
notes.back: B: Client-server.
notes.choices:
A) Peer-to-peer
B) Client-server
C) Distributed network
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: in a peer-to-peer (distributed) network, participants communicate with each other without going through a central point, whereas here every desktop reaches resources on the servers.
notes.explanation: NIST describes local users logging into the server through networked client machines to reach the resources the server provides.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, §5.2 Client/Server Systems, PDF p. 63
notes.evidence: Local users log into the server through networked client machines to access resources that the server provides.

notes.front: What two kinds of link can connect mobile-network base stations to each other, according to NIST?
notes.back: Physical links, such as fibre optic, or wireless links, such as microwave.
notes.explanation: NIST adds that it may be possible to jam the wireless connections that base stations use to talk to each other.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-187, Guide to LTE Security, §4.5.2 Jamming eNodeB Radio Interface, PDF p. 35
notes.evidence: Base stations may have physical (e.g., fiber optic) or wireless (e.g., microwave) links to other base stations. These links are often used to perform call handoff operations. As mentioned in section 4.5.1, it may be possible to jam the wireless connections

notes.front: Which transmission conditions does NIST say make traffic analysis much easier to perform?
notes.back: Part of the path using a wireless network, packets sent over a shared network, or an adversary able to run monitoring tools.
notes.explanation: NIST says these conditions make the attack much easier in practice, not merely possible.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-177 Rev. 1, Trustworthy Email, §3.2 Threats to the Email Infrastructure, PDF p. 33
notes.evidence: especially if part of the email transmission media uses a wireless network, if packets are sent over a shared network, or if the adversary has the ability to run network management or monitoring tools against the victim’s network.

notes.front: In NIST’s virtualisation guidance, what is a virtual network?
notes.back: A software-defined network inside a host that connects the host’s virtual machines to each other and to external networks.
notes.explanation: Configuring this virtual network is one of the administration tasks NIST lists for the virtualised host.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125A Rev. 1, Security Recommendations for Server-based Hypervisor Platforms, §7 Administration of hypervisor, PDF p. 33
notes.evidence: creating and managing hypervisor clusters and configuration of the virtual network inside the hypervisor host. A virtual network is a software-defined network inside the hypervisor host that enables connectivity among VMs, as well as connectivity of VMs to external network (e.g., LAN, WAN, etc.).

notes.front: Two teams’ apps run on the same physical hosts and network. Security wants each team’s app traffic kept apart without laying new cables. What does NIST describe for this?
notes.back: B: A software-defined overlay network that isolates communication between the apps.
notes.choices:
A) A peer-to-peer network between the apps
B) A software-defined overlay network that isolates communication between the apps
C) A second physical network for one team
D) A software-defined wide-area network between the hosts
notes.choicesExplained: A: peer-to-peer describes how participants reach each other, not isolation. C: new cabling is exactly what the team wants to avoid. D: SD-WAN connects sites and users over wide-area links rather than separating apps on one network.
notes.explanation: NIST says an overlay network, the SDN component in most orchestrators, can isolate communication between apps that share the same physical network.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, Application Container Security Guide, §2.3.3 Container technology architecture, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: Most orchestrators also include a software-defined networking (SDN) component known as an overlay network that can be used to isolate communication between apps that share the same physical network.

notes.front: What tight coupling does SD-WAN technology remove?
notes.back: The coupling between the control plane and the data plane functions of the network.
notes.explanation: Removing it lets policies such as access control and routing be specified centrally.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, §5 Secure SD-WAN, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: SD-WAN technology removes the tight coupling between the control plane and data plane functions of the network and enables the centralized specification of various policies, such as access control, routing, and application traffic prioritization.

notes.front: What are two kinds of policy that SD-WAN lets an enterprise specify centrally?
notes.back: Any two of: access control; routing; application traffic prioritisation.
notes.explanation: This central specification follows from separating the control and data plane functions.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, §5 Secure SD-WAN, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: SD-WAN technology removes the tight coupling between the control plane and data plane functions of the network and enables the centralized specification of various policies, such as access control, routing, and application traffic prioritization.

notes.front: What does “extensive connectivity” mean as an SD-WAN design goal?
notes.back: Securely connecting users anywhere to applications and resources hosted anywhere, over any wide-area transport.
notes.explanation: NIST’s examples of transport include broadband internet and 4G or 5G wireless.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, §5.1 Common Requirements for a Secure SD-WAN, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: Extensive connectivity: To securely connect users located anywhere (e.g., home, public location, branch office, corporate office) to applications and resources hosted anywhere (e.g., data center, single or multiple cloud services) using any WAN transport (e.g., MPLS, Broadband Internet, 4G/LTE, 5G wireless)

notes.front: What three things does SD-WAN application awareness weigh when it chooses the best path?
notes.back: The type of network traffic, network load conditions, and the application’s business priority.
notes.explanation: It monitors the traffic and chooses dynamically, so the best path is not fixed in advance.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, §5.1 Common Requirements for a Secure SD-WAN, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: Application awareness: To monitor the network traffic and dynamically choose the best path available based on (a) the type of network traffic, (b) network load conditions, and (c) the application’s business priority.

notes.front: Under SD-WAN centralised visibility and management, what happens to a newly connected appliance?
notes.back: It is recognised and authenticated, then brought under defined management workflows so uniform policies cover all components.
notes.explanation: The aim is one uniform set of policies across all components.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, §5.1 Common Requirements for a Secure SD-WAN, PDF p. 33
notes.evidence: Centralized visibility and management capabilities: Includes the ability to recognize and authenticate newly connected appliances and bring them under the defined management workflows as nodes so as to configure a uniform set of policies that cover all components

notes.front: A retailer’s 200 shops each have broadband and a 5G link. It wants every shop to steer its payment traffic over whichever link is best at the moment, with policies set from one place. Which technology fits?
notes.back: D: A software-defined wide-area network.
notes.choices:
A) A virtual local area network in each shop
B) A demilitarised zone at head office
C) A peer-to-peer network between the shops
D) A software-defined wide-area network
notes.choicesExplained: A: a VLAN groups hosts on switch ports; it does not choose wide-area paths. B: a DMZ holds public-facing servers behind a firewall. C: peer-to-peer describes participants reaching each other directly, with no central policy.
notes.explanation: SD-WAN application awareness picks the best path from traffic type, load and business priority, and SD-WAN allows centralised policies.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, §5.1 Common Requirements for a Secure SD-WAN, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: Application awareness: To monitor the network traffic and dynamically choose the best path available based on (a) the type of network traffic, (b) network load conditions, and (c) the application’s business priority.

notes.front: A firm buys wide-area routers for its branches that also include firewall and secure web gateway functions. Which SD-WAN design goal does this meet?
notes.back: A: Integration of security and networking functions.
notes.choices:
A) Integration of security and networking functions
B) Extensive connectivity
C) Application awareness
D) Centralised visibility and management
notes.choicesExplained: C: application awareness is about choosing paths by traffic type, load and priority. B: extensive connectivity is about reaching resources anywhere over any transport. D: centralised visibility is about recognising and managing appliances under uniform policies.
notes.explanation: NIST’s own example of this goal is a firewall and secure web gateway inside a wide-area router.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, §5.1 Common Requirements for a Secure SD-WAN, PDF p. 33
notes.evidence: Integration of security and networking functions: Use of appliances that contain a combination of networking and security functions (e.g., the presence of a firewall and secure web gateway [SWG] functions in a WAN router)

notes.front: For internet services that run over UDP, such as name lookup and time services, how are the query and the response carried?
notes.back: Each in a single packet, with no connection set up between source and server.
notes.explanation: NIST contrasts this with TCP, which establishes a connection before the exchange.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-189, Resilient Interdomain Traffic Exchange: BGP Security and DDoS Mitigation, §3.2 Reflection Amplification Attacks, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: For internet services that use the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) (e.g., DNS, NTP), the query and response are each contained in a single packet, and the exchange does not require the establishment of a connection between the source and the server (unlike Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)).

notes.front: UDP has no formal process for setting up and ending a connection. What can most stateful inspection firewalls track for it?
notes.back: Only the source and destination IP addresses and ports.
notes.explanation: A UDP packet must still match a state-table entry built from that address and port information before it may pass.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2.1.2 Stateful Inspection, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: Because some protocols, most notably UDP, are connectionless and do not have a formal process for initializing, establishing, and terminating a connection, their state cannot be established at the transport layer as it is for TCP. For these protocols, most firewalls with stateful inspection are only able to track the source and destination IP addresses and ports.

notes.front: A sensor sends a short reading every second. A lost reading does not matter, and the developer wants no connection set-up or delivery acknowledgements. Which transport protocol suits it?
notes.back: B: The User Datagram Protocol.
notes.choices:
A) The Transmission Control Protocol
B) The User Datagram Protocol
C) Secure Shell
D) Internet Protocol Security
notes.choicesExplained: A: TCP provides reliable connection-oriented communications, the set-up and acknowledgements the developer does not want. C: Secure Shell is a protocol for secure administration, not a transport protocol. D: IPsec protects traffic at the network layer; it is not a transport protocol.
notes.explanation: UDP provides unreliable connectionless communications, which matches a sender that tolerates loss and wants no connection.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, §2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: TCP, which provides reliable connection-oriented communications, and the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), which provides unreliable connectionless communications, are commonly used transport layer protocols.

notes.front: Which port does the registry assign to File Transfer Protocol default data?
notes.back: Port 20 (service name ftp-data).
notes.explanation: The File Transfer Protocol’s own entry sits beside it at port 21.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: ftp-data 20 tcp File Transfer [Default Data]

notes.front: Which port does the registry assign to the File Transfer Protocol itself?
notes.back: Port 21 (service name ftp).
notes.explanation: Its default data entry has the port just below, 20.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: ftp 21 tcp File Transfer Protocol

notes.front: Which port does the registry assign to Secure Shell?
notes.back: Port 22 (service name ssh).
notes.explanation: It sits directly below Telnet, at port 23.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: ssh 22 tcp The Secure Shell (SSH)

notes.front: Which port does the registry assign to Telnet?
notes.back: Port 23 (service name telnet).
notes.explanation: NIST’s testing guide gives Telnet as its example of an unsecured protocol.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: telnet 23 tcp Telnet

notes.front: Which port does the registry assign to the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol?
notes.back: Port 25 (service name smtp).
notes.explanation: Mail-reading protocols have their own entries, such as 110 and 143.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: smtp 25 tcp Simple Mail Transfer

notes.front: Which port does the registry assign to the Domain Name System?
notes.back: Port 53, over both TCP and UDP (service name domain).
notes.explanation: The registry lists the service as “Domain Name Server” on both transports.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: domain 53 tcp Domain Name Server [Paul_Mockapetris] [Paul_Mockapetris] domain 53 udp Domain Name Server

notes.front: Which port does the registry assign to web traffic (http)?
notes.back: Port 80 (service name http, described as World Wide Web).
notes.explanation: Web traffic protected by TLS has its own entry at 443.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: http 80 tcp World Wide Web HTTP

notes.front: Which port does the registry assign to Kerberos?
notes.back: Port 88 (service name kerberos).
notes.explanation: The registry lists it over both TCP and UDP.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: kerberos 88 tcp Kerberos [B_Clifford_Neuman] [B_Clifford_Neuman] 2022-02-18 [RFC4120] kerberos 88 udp Kerberos

notes.front: Which port does the registry assign to the Post Office Protocol version 3?
notes.back: Port 110 (service name pop3).
notes.explanation: Its version over TLS has a separate entry at 995.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: pop3 110 tcp Post Office Protocol -

notes.front: Which port does the registry assign to the Internet Message Access Protocol?
notes.back: Port 143 (service name imap).
notes.explanation: Its version over TLS has a separate entry at 993.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: imap 143 tcp Internet Message Access

notes.front: Which port does the registry assign to the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol?
notes.back: Port 389 (service name ldap).
notes.explanation: Its version over TLS has a separate entry at 636.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: ldap 389 tcp Lightweight Directory Access

notes.front: Which port does the registry assign to the Network Time Protocol?
notes.back: Port 123 (service name ntp).
notes.explanation: NIST lists this time service among internet services that run over UDP.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: ntp 123 udp Network Time Protocol

notes.front: Which port does the registry assign to the Trivial File Transfer Protocol?
notes.back: Port 69 (service name tftp).
notes.explanation: Do not confuse it with the File Transfer Protocol at 20 and 21.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: tftp 69 udp Trivial File Transfer

notes.front: Which ports does the registry assign to network management (snmp) and to its traps (snmptrap)?
notes.back: Port 161 for snmp; port 162 for snmptrap.
notes.explanation: The two entries are consecutive, one for the management service and one for its trap messages.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: snmp 161 udp SNMP snmptrap 162 tcp SNMPTRAP

notes.front: Which transport and port does the registry give syslog?
notes.back: UDP port 514.
notes.explanation: At 514 over TCP the registry lists a different service, shell, so the transport matters.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry

notes.front: What does the registry list at port 115, service name sftp?
notes.back: The Simple File Transfer Protocol.
notes.explanation: Despite the name sftp, it is a different protocol from Secure Shell, whose entry is at port 22.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: sftp 115 tcp Simple File Transfer

notes.front: Which UDP port can IKEv2 use to start a new exchange, bypassing UDP port 500 completely?
notes.back: UDP port 4500.
notes.explanation: Starting on 4500 means the exchange avoids UDP port 500 altogether.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, §5.2.4 NAT Traversal, PDF p. 61
notes.evidence: IKEv2 also allows for initiating a new IKE_SA_INIT on UDP port 4500, bypassing UDP port 500 completely.

notes.front: Port 80 versus port 443: what is the difference?
notes.back: 80 carries web (http) traffic; 443 carries http over TLS.
notes.explanation: The registry names the 443 service https.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: https 443 tcp http protocol over TLS/SSL

notes.front: Port 389 versus port 636: what is the difference?
notes.back: 389 carries the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol; 636 carries that protocol over TLS.
notes.explanation: The registry names the 636 service ldaps.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: ldaps 636 tcp ldap protocol over TLS/SSL

notes.front: Port 110 versus port 995: what is the difference?
notes.back: 110 carries the Post Office Protocol version 3; 995 carries it over TLS.
notes.explanation: The registry names the 995 service pop3s.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: pop3s 995 tcp POP3 over TLS protocol

notes.front: Port 143 versus port 993: what is the difference?
notes.back: 143 carries the Internet Message Access Protocol; 993 carries it over TLS.
notes.explanation: The registry names the 993 service imaps.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: imaps 993 tcp IMAP over TLS protocol

notes.front: An audit finds administrators still log in to the core switches with Telnet on port 23. Which change best answers the finding?
notes.back: B: Move to Secure Shell, registered at port 22.
notes.choices:
A) Keep Telnet but move it to a non-standard port
B) Move to Secure Shell, registered at port 22
C) Move to the Trivial File Transfer Protocol on port 69
D) Keep Telnet, because it is on the internal network
notes.choicesExplained: A: a different port does not change the protocol, which stays unsecured. C: the Trivial File Transfer Protocol transfers files; it is not a login protocol. D: NIST counts Telnet as an unsecured protocol that assessments should identify, wherever it runs.
notes.explanation: NIST’s testing guide gives Telnet as its example of an unsecured protocol, and Secure Shell is a secure protocol for administering systems.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-115, Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment, §3.2 Network Sniffing… Review Techniques, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: Identifying operating systems, applications, services, and protocols, including unsecured (e.g., telnet) and unauthorized (e.g., peer-to-peer file sharing) protocols

notes.front: A company’s new mail server must accept mail relayed to it from other organisations’ mail servers. Which port must the firewall allow in?
notes.choicesExplained: A: 110 is the Post Office Protocol version 3, for reading a mailbox. C: 143 is the Internet Message Access Protocol, also for reading mail. D: 993 is that same mail-reading protocol over TLS.
notes.explanation: NIST says email passes from one mail server to another using the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, which the port registry places at 25.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-177 Rev. 1, Trustworthy Email, §2.3.1 Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: Email messages are transferred from one mail server to another (or from an MUA to MSA/MTA) using SMTP.

notes.front: Staff read their mail with the Internet Message Access Protocol. Security now requires that mailbox access be protected with TLS. Which port should the firewall open instead of 143?
notes.choicesExplained: A: 995 is the Post Office Protocol version 3 over TLS, a different mail protocol. C: 636 is the directory protocol over TLS. D: 443 is web traffic over TLS.
notes.explanation: The registry lists port 993 as the Internet Message Access Protocol over TLS.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: imaps 993 tcp IMAP over TLS protocol

notes.front: After a firewall change, servers’ clocks start to drift because they can no longer reach the time servers. Which port and transport should be allowed again?
notes.back: C: UDP port 123.
notes.choices:
A) UDP port 161
B) TCP port 88
C) UDP port 123
D) UDP port 514
notes.choicesExplained: A: 161 is network management (snmp). B: 88 is Kerberos. D: UDP 514 is syslog.
notes.explanation: The registry places the Network Time Protocol at port 123, and it runs over UDP.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
notes.evidence: ntp 123 udp Network Time Protocol

notes.front: Switches must send their log messages by syslog to a central collector, but nothing arrives. The collector’s host firewall allows only TCP port 514. What is wrong?
notes.back: A: Syslog is registered on UDP port 514; TCP 514 is a different service.
notes.choices:
A) Syslog is registered on UDP port 514; TCP 514 is a different service
B) Syslog is registered on TCP port 443
C) Syslog is registered on UDP port 123
D) Nothing: TCP and UDP ports with the same number are the same service
notes.choicesExplained: B: 443 is web traffic over TLS. C: UDP 123 is the Network Time Protocol. D: the registry lists shell, not syslog, at TCP 514, so the transport matters.
notes.explanation: The registry lists syslog under UDP at 514, so allowing only TCP 514 blocks it.
notes.source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (updated 2026-09-11), port registry entry
